page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.u2i-c1m1.3xlarge is an x86_64 compute instance belonging to the ecs.u2i server family, running on the KVM hypervisor. It is equipped with 12 dedicated Intel Xeon vCPUs running at a baseline frequency of 2.7 GHz and 12.0 GB of system memory, providing a 1:1 ratio of 1.0 GB RAM per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated graphics processing units and features no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached storage volumes for persistent data operations.

Networking capabilities feature an 8 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses included by default. The 1:1 vCPU-to-memory configuration distinguishes this tier from standard general-purpose offerings, emphasizing thread density and processor availability over extensive memory capacity. This resource profile optimizes cost efficiency for scenarios where execution threads are demanded continuously without the memory overhead common to 1:2 or 1:4 memory-to-core ratios.

Because the instance lacks local NVMe disks, I/O performance relies on external block storage configurations across the network bus. The ecs.u2i-c1m1.3xlarge is appropriate for compute-bound tasks requiring moderate working memory, such as batch computation, build environments, microservice orchestration, web routing, and distributed worker nodes that perform stateless or compute-heavy processing.

Built with a 1:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio of 1.0 GB RAM per core, this configuration targets multi-threaded compute demands while minimizing excess memory overhead. The server provides an 8 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, does not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses, and features zero local storage, necessitating remote block storage attachments for persistent operations. Furthermore, it operates without GPU hardware accelerators. By delivering high core concurrency relative to its memory allocation, the ecs.u2i-c1m1.3xlarge offers cost-efficient compute capacity for non-memory-intensive workloads, including parallel batch compilation, microservices, continuous integration pipelines, stateless backend processing, and distributed queue worker nodes.
